question: Around which week of pregnancy do the kidneys begin to change?
explanation: Kidney changes start early in the first trimester, around the sixth week of pregnancy, due to hormonal shifts and increased blood volume. [learn more](BMP212_U1_T6#BMP212_U1_T6_h1)

question: Why do the mother's kidneys have to work harder during pregnancy?

options.A: To process waste from both the mother and the baby
options.B: To increase blood pressure for the placenta
options.C: To prevent the bladder from shrinking
options.D: To stop all protein from leaving in the urine

explanation: The maternal kidneys take on extra work to clear out waste products from the growing baby along with the mother's own waste. [learn more](BMP212_U1_T6#BMP212_U1_T6_h1)

question: Which tube carrying urine from the kidney widens more during pregnancy?
explanation: The right ureter widens more than the left because the uterus tilts to the right and the sigmoid colon cushions the left side. [learn more](BMP212_U1_T6#BMP212_U1_T6_h2)

question: What hormone causes the muscles of the urinary tract to relax during pregnancy?
explanation: Progesterone acts as a muscle relaxant, which causes the ureters to widen and urine to flow a bit more slowly. [learn more](BMP212_U1_T6#BMP212_U1_T6_h2)

question: What happens to the rate at which the kidneys filter blood during a normal pregnancy?

options.C: It stops during the third trimester

explanation: The kidney filtration rate rises by up to fifty percent early in pregnancy, meaning the kidneys filter blood much faster. [learn more](BMP212_U1_T6#BMP212_U1_T6_h3)

question: If a pregnant woman's lab results show a creatinine level right in the middle of the normal non-pregnant range, what might this actually mean?
explanation: Normal pregnancy lowers serum creatinine through increased filtration, so a standard non-pregnant value can actually point to reduced kidney function in an expectant mother. [learn more](BMP212_U1_T6#BMP212_U1_T6_h3)

question: What happens to blood sodium levels during a healthy pregnancy?
explanation: Even though total body water increases, a shift in the body's fluid balance causes sodium levels to drop slightly. [learn more](BMP212_U1_T6#BMP212_U1_T6_h4)

question: Why does a pregnant woman's body hold onto several extra litres of fluid?

options.A: High salt intake in her diet
options.B: A resetting of the body's fluid balance center
options.D: Blockage of the main kidney arteries

explanation: The central nervous system adjusts its balance point during pregnancy, encouraging water and sodium retention to build up fluid volume. [learn more](BMP212_U1_T6#BMP212_U1_T6_h4)

question: Why might a pregnant woman have sugar in her urine even when her blood sugar is completely normal?

options.A: Her pancreas has stopped making insulin
options.B: The kidneys filter fluid faster than the tubules can reabsorb the sugar
options.C: Her bladder is leaking stored sugars from meals
options.D: Sugar is made inside the kidneys

explanation: Because the kidneys filter a much higher volume of fluid, small amounts of sugar can slip past reabsorption, which is common and often harmless in pregnancy. [learn more](BMP212_U1_T6#BMP212_U1_T6_h5)

question: When checking mild protein in the urine during an antenatal visit, which statement is incorrect?

options.A: It can sometimes be a normal variation
options.B: It always proves the woman has chronic kidney failure
options.C: It requires checking blood pressure to rule out pre-eclampsia
options.D: It means checking for a urinary tract infection is wise

explanation: Mild protein in the urine does not automatically mean kidney failure; it can be harmless or linked to increased filtration, though it always needs proper clinical follow-up. [learn more](BMP212_U1_T6#BMP212_U1_T6_h5)
